o: Has no body

Its body has been taken over by the axis as the dens.
It is a ring of anterior and posterior arches with lateral masses. (Last's)
Has its transverse ligament attached to the dens

The transverse ligament runs between the lateral masses, behind the dens.
It holds the dens against the anterior arch. (Last's p. 541 - 542, 556)
Has a posterior arch crossed above by the hypoglossal nerve

The vertebral artery and C1 nerve lie in the groove on the upper surface of the posterior arch.
XII leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal, well forward. (Last's p. 541-2)
Has a spinous process

It has only a small posterior tubercle.
This lets the head extend freely. (Last's p. 541, 557)

questions.s: Concerning the axis and its ligaments:
o: The dens unites with the body of the axis at about 12 years

The dens unites with the body of the axis at about 3 years.
Its two half-side centres appear at the fifth fetal month. (Last's)
The alar ligaments attach the dens to the anterior arch of the atlas

The alar ligaments run from the dens to the sides of the foramen magnum (occipital condyles).
They limit rotation. (Last's p. 542)
The apical ligament runs to the posterior margin of the foramen magnum

The apical ligament runs from the tip of the dens to the anterior margin of the foramen magnum.
It is a notochordal remnant. (Last's p. 537)
The tectorial membrane continues the posterior longitudinal ligament upward

It runs from the back of the axis body to the clivus.
It covers the dens and its ligaments from behind. (Last's p. 541, 557)
Bifid spinous processes from C3 to C6

C3–6 spines are short and bifid.
C7 has a long single spine. (Last's p. 557-558)
A foramen transversarium

Each transverse process has a foramen transversarium.
The vertebral artery passes through C6 to C1. (Last's p. 555)
A long spine at C7, the vertebra prominens

C7's spine is the first easily felt in the midline.
The ligamentum nuchae attaches to it. (Last's)
Uncovertebral joints at the sides of the bodies

The lips (uncinate processes) on the sides of the bodies form small joints of Luschka.
Osteophytes here can narrow the intervertebral foramen. (Last's p. 539)
They have no foramina transversaria or costal facets

These features distinguish cervical and thoracic vertebrae.
Lumbar vertebrae have large kidney-shaped bodies instead. (Last's p. 536)
The iliolumbar ligament is attached to the transverse process of L1

The iliolumbar ligament is attached to the transverse process of L5.
Its upper band passes to the iliac crest and gives partial origin to quadratus lumborum. (Last's p. 551-2)
The L5 transverse process joins the vertebra at the junction of pedicle and lamina

The L5 transverse process is short and massive, and its base joins the side of the body itself.
L1–4 processes arise further back, from the pedicle. (Last's p. 550-1)
Their superior articular facets face laterally

Lumbar superior facets face medially (and back), gripping the inferior facets of the vertebra above.
This limits rotation. (Last's p. 551-552)
Has a nucleus pulposus making up about half the disc

The nucleus pulposus is only about 15% of the disc.
The annulus fibrosus makes up the rest. (Last's p. 537)
Is present between the atlas and axis

There is no disc between atlas and axis, or between skull and atlas.
The first disc is between C2 and C3. (Last's p. 537)
Has a nucleus pulposus that is 90% water in old age

It is about 90% water at birth and about 70% in old age.
Young people are about 1 cm taller in the morning. (Last's p. 537)
Prolapses most often posterolaterally

The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and weakest at the sides.
A posterolateral prolapse presses on the nerve root. (Last's p. 539)
The ligamentum flavum is mainly collagen

The ligamentum flavum is mainly yellow elastic tissue.
It helps restore the upright posture after flexion. (Last's p. 539)
The posterior longitudinal ligament is broader over the discs

It is narrow over the bodies and widens over the discs.
Its lateral parts are still weak. (Last's p. 537)
The supraspinous ligament continues into the neck as the ligamentum flavum

It continues upward as the ligamentum nuchae.
The ligamenta flava join the laminae. (Last's p. 539)
The ligamentum nuchae gives attachment to trapezius

Trapezius, splenius and rhomboid minor arise from it.
It runs from C7 to the external occipital protuberance. (Last's p. 544)

questions.s: Concerning the intervertebral foramina and nerve roots:
o: A posterolateral L4/5 disc prolapse usually irritates the L5 nerve root

A disc usually irritates the root one below it: L5 by the L4 disc, S1 by the L5 disc.
The root of the same number has already left, hugging the pedicle above. (Last's p. 539)
The vertebral canal becomes smaller from above downwards

The canal narrows progressively down the column.
It is closed in front by bodies, discs and the PLL. (Last's p. 540)
Each intervertebral foramen is bounded above and below by pedicles

Pedicles form its upper and lower boundaries.
The foramen lodges the spinal nerve, dorsal root ganglion and spinal vessels. (Last's p. 540)
The ligamenta flava close the vertebral canal anteriorly

The ligamenta flava and laminae close the canal posteriorly.
The bodies, discs and posterior longitudinal ligament close it in front. (Last's p. 540)
Is bounded by rectus capitis posterior minor and the two obliques

It is bounded by rectus capitis posterior major and the superior and inferior obliques.
Minor lies medial to it. (Last's p. 546)
Has the greater occipital nerve in its floor

The suboccipital nerve (C1 posterior ramus) lies in the triangle.
The greater occipital nerve (C2) winds round inferior oblique. (Last's p. 546)
Has the anterior arch of the atlas in its floor

Its floor is the posterior arch of the atlas and posterior atlanto-occipital membrane.
The anterior arch lies in front. (Last's p. 546)
Contains the vertebral artery

The vertebral artery lies in the groove on the posterior arch, in the floor of the triangle.
It then pierces the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane. (Last's p. 546)
The needle is inserted at L3/4 or L4/5

These levels lie safely below the end of the cord at L1.
The cauda equina floats away from the needle. (Last's p. 575)
Flexion of the spine opens the spaces between the laminae

Lying on the side with the back flexed separates the spines.
This makes the approach easier. (Last's p. 575)
The needle pierces the ligamentum flavum

Then it pierces dura and arachnoid to enter the subarachnoid space.
A loss of resistance is felt at the ligament. (Last's p. 575)
The needle passes through the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments

It passes through the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments and the ligamentum flavum, then dura and arachnoid.
A loss of resistance is felt as it enters the subarachnoid space. (Last's p. 575)

questions.s: Concerning the nerve supply of back muscles:
o: Erector spinae is supplied by posterior rami

The true (deep) back muscles are supplied segmentally by posterior rami.
They develop from epaxial muscle. (Last's)
Trapezius is supplied by posterior rami

Trapezius is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve, with C3 and C4.
It is a limb muscle that migrated onto the back. (Last's p. 544)
Levator scapulae is supplied by posterior rami

Levator scapulae is supplied by C3, C4 anterior rami and the dorsal scapular nerve.
It is an upper limb muscle. (Last's p. 439)
Serratus posterior superior is supplied by posterior rami

It is supplied by intercostal nerves (anterior rami).
It is a respiratory muscle overlying the true back muscles. (Last's)
The sacral hiatus is due to failure of fusion of the laminae of S1

The hiatus is due to missing laminae of S5 (and often S4).
Its edges are the sacral cornua. (Last's p. 552 - 554)
The dural sac ends at S4

The dural sac ends at S2.
The filum terminale continues down to the coccyx. (Last's p. 574-5)
The sacral canal contains the spinal cord

The canal contains the cauda equina and filum, not the cord.
The cord ends at L1. (Last's p. 575)
The sacral hiatus is used for caudal epidural anaesthesia

Injection through the hiatus reaches the extradural space.
It blocks the sacral nerves. (Last's p. 575)

questions.s: Concerning the joints of the vertebral column:
o: Zygapophyseal joints are synovial

Facet joints are plane synovial joints.
Their orientation sets the movement at each level. (Last's p. 539)
Intervertebral discs form synovial joints

The joints between vertebral bodies are secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses).
There is no joint cavity. (Last's p. 537)
The atlanto-axial joints allow mainly flexion

They allow mainly rotation, about half of all neck rotation.
The dens is the pivot. (Last's p. 542)
The atlanto-occipital joints allow mainly rotation

They allow mainly flexion and extension (nodding).
There is very little rotation. (Last's p. 540 - 543)
